transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

I came in because after nights when I eat like that, I’m left sitting there with crumbs and empty containers everywhere, just ashamed and disgusted with myself. The next morning I can hardly pray or look anyone at church in the eye.
After one of these episodes of eating a large amount of food, do you ever try to get rid of the calories—like making yourself vomit, using laxatives, fasting, or exercising intensely?
I’m not sure what you mean by trying to get rid of the calories. I just feel awful afterward.
After you eat a large amount like that, do you ever make yourself throw up, or skip meals the next day to try to make up for it?
I… I don’t really know. I just know I feel terrible afterward.
After one of these eating episodes, do you ever stick your fingers down your throat or do anything else to make yourself throw up?
I’m not sure. I just feel sick with myself afterward, but I don’t really know what I do to deal with it.
After one of these episodes, do you ever skip meals or eat much less than usual the next day to make up for it?
I’m not really sure. I haven’t paid attention to whether I eat less the next day.
How often would you say these episodes of eating a large amount of food happen—like, how many times a week or month?
Since my friend passed, it’s been at least once or twice most weeks, usually late at night. There hasn’t really been a month where it eased up.
How long ago did your friend pass away, and has this pattern of eating large amounts at night been going on continuously since then?
It’s been about five months now, since my closest bridge partner and church friend died. And yes, it’s been going on since then, pretty continuously.
During these episodes, do you notice yourself eating much faster than usual, or eating until you feel uncomfortably full?
Yes. I eat very fast, usually standing at the kitchen counter. I barely taste the pound cake or crackers, and sometimes I realize I’ve swallowed before I’ve really chewed.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports recurrent episodes of eating large amounts of food (pound cake, crackers) in discrete periods, occurring at least 1-2 times per week for approximately 5 months, temporally linked to grief over her friend's death. Episodes are characterized by eating much more rapidly than normal and until uncomfortably full, occurring in a dissociated/automatic manner (eating before fully aware/chewing). She reports marked subjective distress, shame, guilt, and disgust following episodes, with associated impairment in social/religious functioning (difficulty attending church, facing others). Critically, she denies (or is unaware of) any compensatory behaviors such as self-induced vomiting, laxative use, fasting, or excessive exercise, arguing against bulimia nervosa. There is no reported body image disturbance, fear of weight gain, or restriction driving the episodes, which argues against anorexia/bulimia spectrum. Given the recurrent binge eating with associated distress and no compensatory behavior, this presentation is best classified under ICD-10 F50.8 (Other eating disorders), the category used for Binge Eating Disorder given ICD-10 does not have a distinct code for BED.
